data.name: Garden of Oblivion
data.detailed_description:
One day Reven awakens in a strange but beautiful place where the young teenager is treated like a very special guest. There are talking animals, each being rather kind and friendly. Unless the door is mentioned. The one in the back of the garden. But what could be behind that mysterious door? And why Reven isn’t allowed to go out? You shouldn’t try to know the truth…

Garden of Oblivion is a visual novel/point & click hybrid with horror elements.

  • Move around and question the animals
  • Solve some puzzles and try to unveil the garden's secrets
  • Two different endings are available: Reven's fate is in your hands

It was originally created in a weekend for Ludum Dare 30 with "Connected Worlds" as a theme.

reviews.review:
Garden of Oblivion is a short psychological horror adventure that demonstrates how a small setting and a simple mystery can create an unexpectedly unsettling experience. Developed and published by Träumendes Mädchen, the game combines visual novel storytelling with point-and-click exploration, placing greater emphasis on atmosphere, conversations, and discovery than mechanical complexity. Originally conceived as a game-jam project, it retains the compact structure associated with that origin, yet its limited scale works surprisingly well for the kind of strange, dreamlike story it wants to tell.

The story centers on Reven, a teenager who awakens in an unfamiliar garden with little understanding of how they arrived there. The environment initially seems pleasant rather than threatening, populated by talking animals that welcome Reven and behave with unusual friendliness. That cheerful impression does not last. Toward the rear of the garden stands a mysterious door, and whenever Reven begins asking questions about it, the inhabitants become evasive. Their reluctance to provide straightforward answers immediately raises suspicion and establishes the central mystery. The player is naturally encouraged to investigate precisely because everyone seems determined to discourage it.

Much of the horror comes from this contrast between appearance and implication. Garden of Oblivion does not need an endless supply of monsters or aggressive jump scares to create discomfort. Instead, it makes seemingly harmless conversations feel increasingly suspicious. The garden is colorful and almost comforting, while its inhabitants appear friendly, but there is always a sense that important information is being deliberately concealed. The result is a quieter form of psychological horror in which curiosity becomes the player's main motivation. Every conversation potentially offers another clue about Reven's circumstances and the true nature of the place.

Gameplay follows a straightforward point-and-click adventure structure. Players explore the garden, examine their surroundings, interact with characters, collect information, and solve puzzles needed to advance the mystery. The controls and objectives are generally easy to understand, making the game approachable even for players without extensive experience in traditional adventure games. Its puzzles are not intended to be extremely complicated. They exist primarily to support exploration and provide interaction between narrative moments rather than functioning as elaborate challenges in their own right.

That simplicity can also be considered one of the game's weaknesses. Players looking for intricate puzzles, large environments, extensive inventories, or many hours of exploration will find the experience quite limited. The garden is deliberately small, and the adventure can be completed relatively quickly. There are moments when the premise feels capable of supporting a much larger story, especially because the strange inhabitants and mysterious environment invite further questions. More locations and deeper character interactions could have expanded the mystery considerably. At the same time, extending the game too far might have weakened the concentrated atmosphere that makes its short format effective.

An important element is the presence of two endings. The possibility of reaching different conclusions gives the adventure additional value after the first completion, particularly because knowledge gained during one playthrough can change how the player interprets earlier conversations on another. The branching outcome also complements the themes of curiosity and uncertainty. Instead of presenting the player's investigation as a completely predetermined journey, the game allows Reven's story to conclude in more than one way. Nine Steam achievements provide another incentive for players who enjoy thoroughly exploring short games.

The visual presentation contributes significantly to the unusual tone. Rather than adopting the consistently grim appearance commonly associated with psychological horror, the game uses a whimsical garden and talking animals to disguise its darker qualities. This makes the unsettling moments more effective because they interrupt an environment that initially appears safe. The artwork has the modest character of a small independent project, but its style suits the surreal atmosphere. The result feels closer to an uncomfortable dream or corrupted fairy tale than conventional survival horror.

Its short duration remains the most important consideration before playing. Garden of Oblivion should be approached as a compact narrative experiment rather than a full-scale adventure. There is not enough mechanical or narrative material for players wanting a substantial campaign, but the absence of unnecessary padding means the central mystery remains consistently relevant. Being free to play also makes the limited length far easier to accept. The game can be experienced as a brief horror story that explores an interesting concept without demanding a large investment of either money or time.

Steam Deck compatibility requires some qualification. Garden of Oblivion does not have an official Valve Steam Deck compatibility rating confirming it as Verified or Playable. Its lightweight point-and-click design may make running it through SteamOS and Proton possible, but the lack of an official compatibility classification means handheld users should not assume completely trouble-free operation. Controls may also require trackpad, touchscreen, or custom controller configuration because the original interface is designed around traditional point-and-click interaction. For players who want guaranteed Steam Deck support, its status should therefore be considered unofficial or unverified rather than fully confirmed.

Garden of Oblivion ultimately succeeds by concentrating on a single intriguing situation and allowing suspicion to gradually replace the garden's initial sense of comfort. The mysterious door, evasive talking animals, light puzzles, branching conclusions, and psychological atmosphere combine into a memorable little horror experience. Its simplicity and brevity prevent it from becoming a particularly deep adventure, yet those same qualities make it easy to experience without unnecessary distractions. Players who appreciate unusual indie horror, visual novels, and short point-and-click mysteries are likely to find its strange garden worth exploring.

Rating: 7/10
